malnutrition.n: A medical and humanitarian term for poor health caused by a diet that lacks enough food or the right nutrients. It covers both too little food and an unbalanced diet, so it is wider than hunger, which is simply the feeling or state of needing food. You suffer from malnutrition, and doctors diagnose severe or acute malnutrition. It is uncountable, so say malnutrition is common, never a malnutrition. Related adjective: malnourished.
x: Aid workers say malnutrition is rising sharply in the drought-hit region.
Many of the patients arrived at the clinic suffering from severe malnutrition.

must-have.n: As a noun, it names a product everyone seems to want right now, and it appears constantly in fashion, technology and shopping features. It is informal and often a little promotional. The same spelling works as an adjective before a noun, as in a must-have gadget. Do not confuse it with the verb phrase must have, written as two words, which expresses strong deduction or obligation. Plural: must-haves.
x: The slim leather backpack is this autumn's must-have for commuters.
For many travellers, a portable charger is now a must-have.

nerve-racking.n: Use it for situations that make you tense because something important is at stake, such as exams, interviews, auditions or waiting for results. It describes the experience, not the person, so say the audition was nerve-racking, while you yourself feel nervous. The spelling nerve-wracking is also seen, though nerve-racking is the older, standard form. It is a little stronger than stressful and fits both speech and writing.
x: Waiting for the exam results was the most nerve-racking week of my life.
Giving a speech in front of two hundred strangers is nerve-racking, even for experienced speakers.

networking.n: In business English, this means building a web of professional contacts, usually at events, conferences or online, in the hope of sharing information and finding opportunities. It is uncountable and takes no article. You do networking or go to a networking event. It has positive and slightly calculating overtones, depending on the speaker. In computing it has a separate meaning: connecting computers together.
x: Most of my freelance work comes from networking rather than from advertising.
She dreads networking, but she forced herself to talk to three new people at the conference.

on behalf of.n: A formal phrase meaning that you are speaking or acting as the representative of someone else. It is followed by a person or group: on behalf of the team, on behalf of my client. Speeches, letters and official statements use it a lot. In American English, in behalf of exists with a narrower sense of for the benefit of, but on behalf of is safe everywhere. Do not shorten it to on behalf alone.
x: I am writing on behalf of my employer to confirm your appointment.
The lawyer signed the contract on behalf of her client, who was abroad.

outsource.n: A business verb for paying an outside firm or freelancer to do work that a company could do itself, often to cut costs. It takes the work as its object: outsource customer service, outsource manufacturing. A second pattern adds the place or partner with to or abroad. The noun is outsourcing, and the reverse process, bringing the work back in-house, is often called insourcing. Stress falls on the first syllable: OUT-source.
x: Many small shops outsource their accounting to local firms.
The airline decided to outsource baggage handling to save money.

participate.n: A slightly formal verb for taking part, and it is almost always followed by in, never by to or at. You participate in a discussion, a survey or a race. In everyday speech, take part in is more natural and works in the same frames. The noun is participation and the person is a participant. Stress falls on the second syllable: par-TI-ci-pate. Teachers often ask students to participate more in class.
x: Over a thousand volunteers participate in the beach clean-up every year.
Shy students find it hard to participate in group discussions at first.

persuasive.n: Describes people, arguments or language that are good at making others agree or act. It is positive and focuses on effect, not truth, so a persuasive argument may still be wrong. Common partners include argument, speech, case, essay and evidence. Convincing stresses that something feels believable; persuasive stresses that it moves people to a decision. Persuasive writing is a standard school task, where you argue one side and try to win the reader over.
x: Her persuasive speech convinced the council to fund the new library.
The evidence was strong, but the lawyer's persuasive delivery made the difference.

publicity.n: Media attention given to a person, product or event, whether it is planned or accidental. It is uncountable, so you cannot say a publicity or publicities; use a publicity campaign or a publicity stunt instead. It can be good or bad, and the phrase there is no such thing as bad publicity jokes about the second. Do not confuse it with advertising, which you pay for directly. Publicity is often free, earned coverage.
x: The film's director gave interviews all week to generate publicity before the premiere.
A single viral video gave the small bakery more publicity than years of flyers.

specifications.n: The plural noun for a precise list of requirements or details about how something must be built, made or perform. It is common in engineering, IT and manufacturing, where a contract may require work to the client's specifications. Informally it shortens to specs, as in a phone's specs. The singular specification can mean one such detail or the whole document. The verb is specify, with stress on SPEC.
x: Please check the technical specifications before you order the replacement part.
The new laptop has impressive specifications, but the battery life is disappointing.

thought-provoking.n: Praise for a book, film, talk or question that sets you thinking about ideas, not just entertains you. It is hyphenated and normally goes before a noun or after be: a thought-provoking essay, the lecture was thought-provoking. It suggests depth without necessarily meaning the work is enjoyable or that you agree with it. Reviewers use it often, so in your own writing try to say what the work makes you think about.
x: The play raises thought-provoking questions about family loyalty.
I found the exhibition thought-provoking, although I disagreed with some of its claims.

tranquil.n: A literary, slightly formal word for places or moments that are calm, quiet and free from disturbance. Typical nouns are lake, garden, village, scene and atmosphere. It is stronger and more poetic than quiet, and it is common in travel writing and hotel descriptions. The noun is tranquillity in British English and often tranquility in American English. Both spellings of the noun are correct; the adjective is the same in each.
x: The hotel garden is a tranquil place to read in the afternoon.
After the noisy city, the tranquil mountain lake felt almost unreal.

turn up.n: This phrasal verb has two common senses. Intransitively, it means to arrive or appear, often without much warning or after a delay: nobody turned up. Transitively, it means to increase volume, heat or brightness, and there the particle can sit after the object: turn the music up, or turn up the music. With a pronoun, the particle must follow it: turn it up. The arriving sense is informal and never takes an object.
x: Half of the guests didn't turn up, so we had far too much food.
Could you turn up the heating? It's freezing in here.

weather permitting.n: A fixed formal phrase placed at the start or end of a plan to say that it will go ahead only if conditions are good. It is a reduced clause equal to if the weather permits, and it is common in announcements, schedules and invitations. Keep it as a block; there is no need for a subject or tense. It is used for outdoor events such as flights, picnics, matches and ceremonies, and it is polite and slightly official in tone.
x: Weather permitting, the ferry will leave at nine tomorrow morning.
We plan to hold the wedding in the garden, weather permitting.

without further ado.n: A speaker's formula that signals the introduction is over and the main event begins. It is common at the start of presentations, ceremonies, shows and videos, and it is a little formal or theatrical. Ado means fuss or delay, an old word that survives mainly in this phrase and in much ado about nothing. It sits at the start of a sentence and is followed by a comma. It sounds odd in ordinary conversation between friends.
x: Without further ado, let me hand over to our guest of honour.
I know you're all hungry, so without further ado, let's cut the cake.

guild.n: In history, a medieval association of merchants or craftworkers who set standards, protected members and controlled their trade in a town. Weavers, bakers and goldsmiths each had their own guild. Today the word survives in names of professional bodies, such as a writers' guild, and in online games where players form a team. It is pronounced like gild, with a hard g, and it rhymes with build. Do not confuse it with guilt, which is a feeling.
x: Only members of the weavers' guild could sell cloth in the town market.
In the game, our guild meets every Friday to plan the next raid.

look up to.n: A three-word phrasal verb meaning to admire and respect someone, usually a person who is older, wiser or more experienced. It is always transitive and inseparable, so the object comes after to: she looks up to her coach. Do not say look up someone to mean admire; look someone up means to search for them. The opposite is look down on, which means to regard someone as inferior. It is natural in everyday speech and writing.
x: Teenagers often look up to athletes who speak honestly about their struggles.
He will always look up to his older brother, whatever he does.

redundancy.n: In British English, redundancy means losing your job because the employer no longer needs the role, not because of poor performance. It can be countable (hundreds of redundancies) or uncountable. Typical phrases: voluntary redundancy, redundancy pay, be made redundant. American English prefers layoff for the same event. There is also a general meaning of unnecessary repetition, as in a redundancy in a sentence.
x: After the merger, fifty jobs in the sales department were put at risk of redundancy.
She took voluntary redundancy and used the payment to start her own business.

reject.n: A verb for refusing to accept something such as an offer, idea, application or request. It is stronger and more final than decline, which sounds politer, and it often involves a formal decision. A person, a committee or even a body can be the subject, and the thing rejected is the object. It is stressed on the second syllable: re-JECT. The noun, with stress on the first syllable, means a rejected product or person, and it can sound offensive when used of people.
x: The bank rejected her loan application because of her unstable income.
Voters overwhelmingly rejected the plan to close the local hospital.

release.n: A flexible verb with two main groups of meaning. It can mean to let someone or something go, as in release a prisoner or release gas, and to make something available to the public, as in release an album, a film or a statement. Both verb and noun are stressed on the second syllable, re-LEASE, and the noun appears in a press release or a new release. Typical objects include prisoners, data, a report and a software update.
x: The studio will release the sequel in cinemas next summer.
Police released the man without charge after questioning him for several hours.

revise.n: Has two main senses that differ by variety of English. In general use, it means to change something, such as a plan or estimate, to correct or improve it. In British English, it also means to review your notes before an exam, where Americans say study or review. You revise for an exam in British usage, but you revise a document everywhere. The noun is revision. Stress is on the second syllable: re-VISE.
x: The author revised the manuscript three times before sending it to the publisher.
I have to revise for my chemistry test all weekend.

to date.n: A formal phrase meaning up to now, used in reports and news about progress. It usually begins or ends a sentence, and it is typically paired with the present perfect: to date, we have received. It suggests that the situation may change later. So far is the everyday equivalent, and thus far is more formal. Do not confuse it with up to date, an adjective meaning current, which is not the same as the adverbial phrase here.
x: To date, the museum has welcomed more than two million visitors.
The company has raised ten million dollars to date.

carry-on.n: As an adjective, it describes a bag small enough to take into the airplane cabin, and it is mainly American. In British English, hand luggage or cabin bag is more usual. As a noun, a carry-on is the bag itself, and carry-on baggage is the full phrase. The hyphen is standard before a noun, as in a carry-on bag. In British English, a carry-on can also mean an annoying fuss, which is a different informal sense.
x: I travel with only a carry-on bag to avoid waiting at the luggage belt.
Liquids in your carry-on luggage must be in containers of 100 ml or less.

crossroads.n: A place where two or more roads meet. Although it ends in s, it is usually treated as singular: the crossroads is dangerous, though the plural is the same. Usage in directions is common: turn left at the crossroads. In British English, junction is the broader word, and American English prefers intersection. Figuratively, being at a crossroads means facing an important decision that will shape your future, as in a career or relationship.
x: Go straight until you reach the crossroads, then turn left at the petrol station.
At 40, she found herself at a crossroads and decided to change careers.
